title: Der Grabhügel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 195. Text from Wikisource („Der Grabhügel (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 195 opens with a rich farmer looking over his fields, his fattened cattle and his iron money-chests when a knocking begins — not at the door of his room but at the door of his heart, which answers every question it is asked against him. The one mercy he manages, eight measures of grain given to a starving neighbour, comes with a condition attached: three nights’ watch at his grave. The third night brings a scarred, discharged soldier who says of himself that he is like the boy who went out to find out what fear was and never did, and the trick he plays — a riding boot with the sole cut away, set over a half-overgrown pit — keeps the devil pouring gold into it until sunrise.

sentences.t: Ein reicher Bauer stand eines Tags in seinem Hof und schaute nach seinen Feldern und Gärten: das Korn wuchs kräftig heran und die Obstbäume hiengen voll Früchte.
sentences.l: A rich farmer stood one day in his yard and looked out over his fields and gardens: the grain was growing up sturdily and the fruit-trees hung full of fruit.
sentences.i: A rich farmer stood in his yard one day and looked out over his fields and gardens: the corn was coming on strongly and the fruit trees hung full of fruit.
sentences.n: “eines Tags” is a genitive of time — German marks “one day” by case rather than by a preposition. “heranwachsen” is separable, and the particle “heran” has drifted to the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Das Getraide des vorigen Jahrs lag noch in so mächtigen Haufen auf dem Boden, daß es kaum die Balken tragen konnten.
sentences.l: The grain of the previous year lay still in such mighty heaps on the floor that the beams could scarcely carry it.
sentences.i: Last year’s grain still lay in such mighty heaps on the floor that the beams could scarcely bear it.
sentences.n: “Getraide” is the 1857 spelling of Getreide. “Boden” here is the loft floor of the barn, which is why the beams are the ones taking the weight.

sentences.t: Dann gieng er in den Stall, da standen die gemästeten Ochsen, die fetten Kühe und die spiegelglatten Pferde.
sentences.l: Then went he into the stable, there stood the fattened oxen, the fat cows and the mirror-smooth horses.
sentences.i: Then he went into the stable, where the fattened oxen stood, and the fat cows, and the horses with coats like glass.
sentences.n: “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging. “spiegelglatt” — smooth as a mirror; German builds the comparison into one word.

sentences.t: Endlich gieng er in seine Stube zurück und warf seine Blicke auf die eisernen Kasten, in welchen sein Geld lag.
sentences.l: At last went he back into his parlour and threw his glances on the iron chests in which his money lay.
sentences.i: At last he went back into his parlour and cast his eye over the iron chests in which his money lay.
sentences.n: “Blicke werfen auf” is to cast a look at. “welchen” after a preposition is the older relative pronoun where modern German would as readily use “denen”.

sentences.t: Als er so stand, und seinen Reichthum übersah, klopfte es auf einmal heftig bei ihm an.
sentences.l: As he stood so, and surveyed his riches, there knocked it all at once loudly at his door.
sentences.i: As he stood there taking in his riches, all at once there came a loud knock.
sentences.n: “es klopfte bei ihm an” is impersonal: German lets “es” stand as the subject and names no knocker — which is the point of the sentence that follows. “Reichthum” is the 1857 spelling of Reichtum.

sentences.t: Es klopfte aber nicht an die Thüre seiner Stube, sondern an die Thüre seines Herzens.
sentences.l: It knocked however not at the door of his parlour, but at the door of his heart.
sentences.i: But it was not at the door of his parlour that it knocked; it was at the door of his heart.
sentences.n: “sondern” is the “but” that corrects a negative. “Thüre” is the 1857 spelling of Türe.

sentences.t: Sie that sich auf und er hörte eine Stimme, die zu ihm sprach „hast du den Deinigen damit wohl gethan?
sentences.l: It opened itself and he heard a voice that said to him “have you done well by your own with it?
sentences.i: It opened, and he heard a voice that said to him, “have you done well by your own people with it?
sentences.n: “sie” is the door, feminine in German. “that … auf” is aufthun (modern auftun), to open; “that” is the 1857 spelling of tat.

sentences.t: hast du die Noth der Armen angesehen? hast du mit den Hungrigen dein Brot getheilt?
sentences.l: have you looked upon the distress of the poor? have you shared your bread with the hungry?
sentences.i: have you looked on the need of the poor? have you shared your bread with the hungry?
sentences.n: “Noth” is the 1857 spelling of Not. “ansehen” here is not just to see but to look on at something without acting.

sentences.t: war dir genug was du besaßest oder hast du noch immer mehr verlangt?“
sentences.l: was enough for you what you possessed, or have you always demanded still more?”
sentences.i: was what you had ever enough for you, or have you always wanted more?”
sentences.n: “besaßest” is the past of besitzen with the old -est ending for “du”. “war dir genug” — the dative names the person for whom it was enough.

sentences.t: Das Herz zögerte nicht mit der Antwort „ich bin hart und unerbittlich gewesen und habe den Meinigen niemals etwas Gutes erzeigt.
sentences.l: The heart did not hesitate with the answer “I have been hard and unrelenting and have never shown my own people anything good.
sentences.i: The heart did not hesitate with its answer: “I have been hard and unrelenting, and I never did my own people a kindness.
sentences.n: “die Meinigen” are one’s own family and household — the substantivized possessive used of people. The heart answers in the man’s own voice.

sentences.t: Ist ein Armer gekommen, so habe ich mein Auge weg gewendet.
sentences.l: Has a poor man come, then have I turned my eye away.
sentences.i: If a poor man came, I turned my eye away.
sentences.n: A conditional with the verb first and no “wenn” — the same move English makes in “had he come”. “weg gewendet” is printed as two words for modern weggewendet.

sentences.t: Ich habe mich um Gott nicht bekümmert, sondern nur an die Mehrung meines Reichthums gedacht.
sentences.l: I have not concerned myself about God, but thought only of the increase of my riches.
sentences.i: I never troubled myself about God, but thought only of increasing my riches.
sentences.n: “sich um etwas bekümmern” is to concern oneself with something. “Mehrung” is the older noun of mehren, to increase.

sentences.t: Wäre alles mein eigen gewesen, was der Himmel bedeckte, dennoch hätte ich nicht genug gehabt.“
sentences.l: Had everything been my own that the sky covered, still would I not have had enough.”
sentences.i: Had everything under heaven been my own, I still would not have had enough.”
sentences.n: “mein eigen” stands uninflected after the noun, an older usage kept for solemnity. “was der Himmel bedeckte” — all that the sky covers, a set phrase for everything on earth.

sentences.t: Als er diese Antwort vernahm, erschrack er heftig: die Knie fiengen an ihm zu zittern und er mußte sich niedersetzen.
sentences.l: When he heard this answer, he took fright violently: the knees began to tremble on him and he had to sit himself down.
sentences.i: When he heard this answer he was violently afraid: his knees began to tremble under him, and he had to sit down.
sentences.n: “die Knie fiengen an ihm zu zittern” — the dative “ihm” says whose knees they are, where English uses a possessive. “erschrack” is the 1857 spelling of erschrak.

sentences.t: Da klopfte es abermals an, aber es klopfte an die Thüre seiner Stube.
sentences.l: Then knocked it once again, but it knocked at the door of his parlour.
sentences.i: Then there came another knock, but this time at the door of his parlour.
sentences.n: The same impersonal “es klopfte an” as before, and the contrast with the earlier knock is the whole point of repeating it.

sentences.t: Es war sein Nachbar, ein armer Mann, der ein Häufchen Kinder hatte, die er nicht mehr sättigen konnte.
sentences.l: It was his neighbour, a poor man who had a little heap of children whom he could no longer satisfy.
sentences.i: It was his neighbour, a poor man with a whole little heap of children that he could no longer feed.
sentences.n: “ein Häufchen Kinder” — a little heap of children; the diminutive -chen makes it affectionate rather than dismissive. “sättigen” is to fill, to satisfy hunger.

sentences.t: „Ich weiß,“ dachte der Arme, „mein Nachbar ist reich, aber er ist ebenso hart:
sentences.l: “I know,” thought the poor man, “my neighbour is rich, but he is just as hard:
sentences.i: “I know,” thought the poor man, “my neighbour is rich, but he is just as hard;
sentences.n: “weiß” here is the verb wissen, to know, not the adjective “white” with the same spelling — the surrounding words are what tell them apart.

sentences.t: ich glaube nicht daß er mir hilft, aber meine Kinder schreien nach Brot, da will ich es wagen.“
sentences.l: I do not believe that he helps me, but my children cry for bread, so will I risk it.”
sentences.i: I do not believe he will help me, but my children are crying for bread, so I will risk it.”
sentences.n: German uses the present “hilft” where English needs the future. “es wagen” is to venture it, to chance it — the verb wagen, not the noun Wagen, cart.

sentences.t: Er sprach zu dem Reichen „Ihr gebt nicht leicht etwas von dem eurigen weg, aber ich stehe da wie einer, dem das Wasser bis an den Kopf geht: meine Kinder hungern, leiht mir vier Malter Korn.“
sentences.l: He said to the rich man “you do not easily give away anything of what is yours, but I stand here like one to whom the water goes up to the head: my children are hungry, lend me four Malter of grain.”
sentences.i: He said to the rich man, “you do not readily give away anything of your own, but I stand here like a man with the water up to his neck: my children are hungry, lend me four Malter of grain.”
sentences.n: “ihr” is the older respectful address to one person. “dem das Wasser bis an den Kopf geht” is the German form of the picture English draws at the neck; a Malter was a grain measure of several bushels.

sentences.t: Der Reiche sah ihn lange an, da begann der erste Sonnenstrahl der Milde einen Tropfen von dem Eis der Habsucht abzuschmelzen.
sentences.l: The rich man looked at him a long time, then began the first sunbeam of mildness to melt off a drop from the ice of avarice.
sentences.i: The rich man looked at him a long while, and then the first ray of mercy began to melt one drop from the ice of his greed.
sentences.n: “Milde” here is the noun, mildness or mercy, in the genitive after “Sonnenstrahl”. “abschmelzen” is separable, and the zu-infinitive puts the “zu” inside the verb: abzuschmelzen.

sentences.t: „Vier Malter will ich dir nicht leihen,“ antwortete er, „sondern achte will ich dir schenken, aber eine Bedingung mußt du erfüllen.“
sentences.l: “Four Malter will I not lend you,” he answered, “but eight will I give you, only one condition must you fulfil.”
sentences.i: “Four Malter I will not lend you,” he answered, “but eight I will give you outright — only you must meet one condition.”
sentences.n: “achte” here is the numeral eight, inflected to agree with the unspoken Malter, not the verb achten. “schenken” means to give as a gift, not to lend, and the contrast with “leihen” is the whole offer.

sentences.t: „Was soll ich thun?“ sprach der Arme.
sentences.l: “What shall I do?” said the poor man.
sentences.n: “thun” is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: „Wenn ich todt bin, sollst du drei Nächte an meinem Grabe wachen.“
sentences.l: “When I am dead, you shall watch three nights at my grave.”
sentences.n: “todt” is the 1857 spelling of tot. “wachen” is to keep watch, to stay awake — the tale’s central act.

sentences.t: Dem Bauer ward bei dem Antrag unheimlich zu Muth, doch in der Noth, in der er sich befand, hätte er alles bewilligt: er sagte also zu und trug das Korn heim.
sentences.l: To the farmer became at the proposal uncanny in mood, yet in the distress in which he found himself he would have granted anything: he said yes then and carried the grain home.
sentences.i: The proposal made the farmer’s flesh creep, yet in the straits he was in he would have agreed to anything; so he said yes and carried the grain home.
sentences.n: “ward” is the old past of werden. “einem wird unheimlich zu Muth” is a set phrase built on the dative: the mood comes over the person rather than being had by him. The poor neighbour is called “der Bauer” too from here on — the rich man of the opening is dead by the next paragraph, and the word passes to the man who is left.

sentences.t: Es war, als hätte der Reiche vorausgesehen was geschehen würde, nach drei Tagen fiel er plötzlich todt zur Erde; man wußte nicht recht wie es zugegangen war, aber niemand trauerte um ihn.
sentences.l: It was as if the rich man had foreseen what would happen; after three days he fell suddenly dead to the earth; one did not rightly know how it had come about, but nobody mourned for him.
sentences.i: It was as though the rich man had foreseen what would happen: three days later he fell down dead, and no one rightly knew how it had come about, but nobody mourned him.
sentences.n: “als hätte” takes the subjunctive with no “wenn” and the verb first — the ordinary German for “as though”. “zugehen” is used impersonally of how something came to pass.

sentences.t: Als er bestattet war, fiel dem Armen sein Versprechen ein:
sentences.l: When he was buried, the poor man remembered his promise:
sentences.i: When he had been buried, the poor man remembered his promise:
sentences.n: “einfallen” works the other way round from English remembering: the promise falls in to him, so the person stands in the dative (“dem Armen”).

sentences.t: gerne wäre er davon entbunden gewesen, aber er dachte „er hat sich gegen dich doch mildthätig erwiesen, du hast mit seinem Korn deine hungrigen Kinder gesättigt,
sentences.l: gladly would he have been released from it, but he thought “he has after all shown himself charitable toward you, you have satisfied your hungry children with his grain,
sentences.i: he would gladly have been let off it, but he thought, “he did prove charitable to you after all; you fed your hungry children with his grain,
sentences.n: “entbinden” is to loose someone from an obligation. “mildthätig” — charitable, literally “doing mildly”; the -th- is the 1857 spelling.

sentences.t: und wäre das auch nicht, du hast einmal das Versprechen gegeben und mußt du es halten.“
sentences.l: and were that not so either, you have once given the promise and must you keep it.”
sentences.i: and even were that not so, you gave your promise once, and keep it you must.”
sentences.n: The printing has “und mußt du es halten”, with the subject repeated after the verb as if a new sentence were starting. We keep the anacoluthon rather than tidying it; the idiomatic line renders the emphasis it produces.

sentences.t: Bei einbrechender Nacht gieng er auf den Kirchhof und setzte sich auf den Grabhügel.
sentences.l: At falling night he went to the churchyard and set himself on the grave-mound.
sentences.i: At nightfall he went to the churchyard and seated himself on the grave-mound.
sentences.n: “bei einbrechender Nacht” uses a present participle where English uses a noun: at nightfall. “sich setzen” always needs the reflexive pronoun.

sentences.t: Es war alles still, nur der Mond schien über die Grabhügel und manchmal flog eine Eule vorbei und ließ ihre kläglichen Töne hören.
sentences.l: It was all quiet, only the moon shone over the grave-mounds and sometimes an owl flew past and let its plaintive notes be heard.
sentences.i: All was quiet; only the moon shone over the grave-mounds, and now and then an owl flew past and let its plaintive notes be heard.
sentences.n: “hören lassen” — to let something be heard, German’s way of saying that a sound was uttered. “kläglich” is plaintive, lamenting.

sentences.t: Als die Sonne aufgieng, begab sich der Arme ungefährdet heim, und ebenso gieng die zweite Nacht ruhig vorüber.
sentences.l: When the sun went up, the poor man betook himself home unendangered, and just so went the second night quietly by.
sentences.i: When the sun rose the poor man made his way home unharmed, and the second night passed just as quietly.
sentences.n: “aufgehen” of the sun is to rise. “sich begeben” is to betake oneself somewhere, an elevated way of saying “to go”.

sentences.t: Den Abend des dritten Tages empfand er eine besondere Angst, es war ihm als stände noch etwas bevor.
sentences.l: The evening of the third day he felt a peculiar fear, it was to him as if something were still at hand.
sentences.i: On the evening of the third day he felt a strange dread; it seemed to him that something was still to come.
sentences.n: “Den Abend” is a bare accusative of time — no preposition needed. “bevorstehen” is to lie ahead, to be in store, and “stände” is its subjunctive of report.

sentences.t: Als er hinaus kam, erblickte er an der Mauer des Kirchhofs einen Mann, den er noch nie gesehen hatte.
sentences.l: When he came out, he caught sight by the wall of the churchyard of a man whom he had never yet seen.
sentences.i: When he came out he caught sight of a man by the churchyard wall whom he had never seen before.
sentences.n: “noch nie” is the double-marked “never yet” German prefers where English is content with one negative word.

sentences.t: Er war nicht mehr jung, hatte Narben im Gesicht und seine Augen blickten scharf und feurig umher.
sentences.l: He was no longer young, had scars in the face and his eyes looked about sharply and fierily.
sentences.i: He was no longer young; he had scars on his face, and his eyes went about sharp and fiery.
sentences.n: “Narben im Gesicht” — German says “in the face” where English says “on”. “feurig” is fiery, from Feuer.

sentences.t: Er war ganz von einem alten Mantel bedeckt und nur große Reiterstiefeln waren sichtbar.
sentences.l: He was covered entirely by an old cloak and only large riding-boots were visible.
sentences.i: He was covered all over by an old cloak, and only a pair of big riding-boots showed.
sentences.n: “Reiterstiefeln” keeps the older plural in -n. The boots are the tale’s hinge, and the printing plants them here without a word of explanation.

sentences.t: „Was sucht ihr hier?“ redete ihn der Bauer an, „gruselt euch nicht auf dem einsamen Kirchhof?“
sentences.l: “What are you looking for here?” the farmer addressed him, “do you not feel the creeps in the lonely churchyard?”
sentences.i: “What are you after here?” the farmer said to him. “Does the lonely churchyard not give you the creeps?”
sentences.n: “anreden” is separable: “redete ihn … an”. “gruseln” is impersonal — the creeping dread comes over you, so the person stands in the accusative (“euch”).

sentences.t: „Ich suche nichts,“ antwortete er, „aber ich fürchte auch nichts.
sentences.l: “I am looking for nothing,” he answered, “but I also fear nothing.
sentences.i: “I am after nothing,” he answered, “but I fear nothing either.
sentences.n: German uses the plain present where English needs the progressive: “ich suche” covers both “I seek” and “I am seeking”.

sentences.t: Ich bin wie der Junge, der ausgieng das Gruseln zu lernen, und sich vergeblich bemühte,
sentences.l: I am like the lad who went out to learn shuddering, and took pains in vain,
sentences.i: I am like the lad who went out to learn how to shudder, and took all that trouble for nothing,
sentences.n: The soldier is pointing at another tale in this same collection, the boy who set out to learn what fear was. The 1857 text expects the reader to know it and explains nothing.

sentences.t: der aber bekam die Königstochter zur Frau und mit ihr große Reichthümer, und ich bin immer arm geblieben.
sentences.l: but he got the king’s daughter for a wife and with her great riches, and I have always remained poor.
sentences.i: but he got the king’s daughter to wife, and great riches with her, while I have stayed poor all along.
sentences.n: “der aber” — a demonstrative restarting the sentence about the same lad, which is why the German can carry on without a new subject. “zur Frau bekommen” is to get someone in marriage.

sentences.t: Ich bin nichts als ein abgedankter Soldat und will hier die Nacht zubringen, weil ich sonst kein Obdach habe.“
sentences.l: I am nothing but a discharged soldier and want to pass the night here, because I have no other shelter.”
sentences.i: I am nothing but a discharged soldier, and I mean to pass the night here because I have no other roof.”
sentences.n: “abgedankt” is the word for a soldier let go from service. “zubringen” is separable: to spend, of time.

sentences.t: „Wenn ihr keine Furcht habt,“ sprach der Bauer, „so bleibt bei mir und helft mir dort den Grabhügel bewachen.“
sentences.l: “If you have no fear,” said the farmer, “then stay with me and help me guard the grave-mound over there.”
sentences.i: “If you have no fear,” said the farmer, “then stay with me and help me keep watch on that grave-mound.”
sentences.n: “Furcht haben” — German has fear rather than being afraid. “bewachen” is transitive, to guard something.

sentences.t: „Wacht halten ist Sache des Soldaten“ antwortete er, „was uns hier begegnet, Gutes oder Böses, das wollen wir gemeinschaftlich tragen.“
sentences.l: “Keeping watch is the soldier’s business,” he answered, “what meets us here, good or bad, that will we bear jointly.”
sentences.i: “Keeping watch is a soldier’s business,” he answered. “Whatever meets us here, good or bad, we will bear it together.”
sentences.n: “Sache des Soldaten” — a bare genitive where English uses “a soldier’s”. “Gutes oder Böses” are adjectives used as nouns, and the resumptive “das” gathers them up before the verb.

sentences.t: Der Bauer schlug ein und sie setzten sich zusammen auf das Grab.
sentences.l: The farmer struck in and they sat down together on the grave.
sentences.i: The farmer struck hands on it, and they sat down together on the grave.
sentences.n: “einschlagen” is to strike hands on a bargain — the gesture that seals an agreement.

sentences.t: Alles blieb still bis Mitternacht, da ertönte auf einmal ein schneidendes Pfeifen in der Luft, und die beiden Wächter erblickten den Bösen, der leibhaftig vor ihnen stand.
sentences.l: Everything stayed quiet until midnight, then rang out all at once a cutting whistling in the air, and the two watchers caught sight of the Evil One, who stood bodily before them.
sentences.i: All stayed quiet until midnight; then all at once a cutting whistle rang through the air, and the two watchers caught sight of the Evil One, standing there before them in the flesh.
sentences.n: “der Böse” — the Wicked One — is one of the tale’s several names for the devil, and it is the adjective böse used as a noun. “leibhaftig” is in the body, in person.

sentences.t: „Fort, ihr Halunken,“ rief er ihnen zu, „der in dem Grab liegt, ist mein: ich will ihn holen, und wo ihr nicht weg geht, dreh ich euch die Hälse um.“
sentences.l: “Away, you scoundrels,” he called to them, “the one who lies in the grave is mine: I mean to fetch him, and if you do not go away, I will twist your necks round.”
sentences.i: “Off with you, you scoundrels,” he called to them, “the man lying in that grave is mine; I mean to fetch him, and if you do not go, I will wring your necks.”
sentences.n: “wo” here is the older “if, in case”, not “where”. “dreh … um” is umdrehen, to twist round; the particle closes the clause.

sentences.t: „Herr mit der rothen Feder,“ sprach der Soldat, „ihr seid mein Hauptmann nicht, ich brauch euch nicht zu gehorchen, und das Fürchten hab ich noch nicht gelernt.
sentences.l: “Sir with the red feather,” said the soldier, “you are not my captain, I do not need to obey you, and fearing I have not yet learnt.
sentences.i: “Sir with the red feather,” said the soldier, “you are not my captain; I need not obey you, and I have not yet learnt how to be afraid.
sentences.n: The red feather in the hat is the devil’s mark in these tales, and the soldier names him by it instead of by his name. “das Fürchten” is the infinitive used as a noun — the same construction as the other tale’s “das Gruseln”.

sentences.t: Geht eurer Wege, wir bleiben hier sitzen.“
sentences.l: Go your ways, we stay sitting here.”
sentences.i: Go your way; we stay where we are.”
sentences.n: “eurer Wege” is an old genitive of direction that survives only in this phrase. “bleiben sitzen” — to remain seated, German pairing two plain verbs where English adds a participle.

sentences.t: Der Teufel dachte „mit Gold fängst du die zwei Haderlumpen am besten,“
sentences.l: The devil thought “with gold you catch the two ragamuffins best,”
sentences.i: The devil thought, “gold is the best way to catch these two ragamuffins,”
sentences.n: German states a general rule with “du” where English says “one” or turns the sentence round. “Haderlumpen” — Hader and Lumpen both mean rag, and the compound is thrown at people, not at cloth.

sentences.t: zog gelindere Saiten auf und fragte ganz zutraulich ob sie nicht einen Beutel mit Gold annehmen und damit heim gehen wollten.
sentences.l: drew gentler strings up and asked quite confidingly whether they would not accept a purse with gold and go home with it.
sentences.i: tuned his strings to a gentler pitch, and asked in a friendly way whether they would not take a purse of gold and go home with it.
sentences.n: “gelindere Saiten aufziehen” is to restring an instrument more softly — the German picture for changing one’s tone. “ob” sends its verb to the end.

sentences.t: „Das läßt sich hören,“ antwortete der Soldat, „aber mit Einem Beutel voll Gold ist uns nicht gedient:
sentences.l: “That lets itself be heard,” answered the soldier, “but with one single purse full of gold we are not served:
sentences.i: “Now that is worth hearing,” answered the soldier, “but a single purse of gold is no use to us:
sentences.n: “Einem” is printed with a capital to stress the numeral: one purse only. “damit ist uns nicht gedient” is impersonal — that does not serve our turn.

sentences.t: wenn ihr so viel Gold geben wollt als da in einen von meinen Stiefeln geht, so wollen wir Euch das Feld räumen und abziehen.“
sentences.l: if you will give as much gold as goes in there into one of my boots, then will we clear the field for you and march off.”
sentences.i: if you will give as much gold as will go into one of my boots, we will leave you the field and march off.”
sentences.n: “das Feld räumen” is to quit the field, the loser’s move in a battle — soldier’s language throughout the bargain. The printed “Euch” is capitalised where the same word is small elsewhere in the tale.

sentences.t: „So viel habe ich nicht bei mir,“ sagte der Teufel, „aber ich will es holen:
sentences.l: “So much have I not with me,” said the devil, “but I will fetch it:
sentences.i: “I have not so much on me,” said the devil, “but I will fetch it:
sentences.n: “bei mir haben” — to have about one, on one’s person.

sentences.t: in der benachbarten Stadt wohnt ein Wechsler, der mein guter Freund ist, der streckt mir gerne so viel vor.“
sentences.l: in the neighbouring town lives a money-changer who is my good friend, he advances me so much gladly.”
sentences.i: in the next town there lives a money-changer who is a good friend of mine; he will gladly advance me that much.”
sentences.n: “vorstrecken” is to advance money; the particle “vor” stands at the end. A Wechsler dealt in coin and credit, the moneylender of an age before banks.

sentences.t: Als der Teufel verschwunden war, zog der Soldat seinen linken Stiefel aus und sprach „dem Kohlenbrenner wollen wir schon eine Nase drehen: gebt mir nur euer Messer, Gevatter.“
sentences.l: When the devil had vanished, the soldier pulled off his left boot and said “the charcoal-burner we will play a trick on: only give me your knife, godfather.”
sentences.i: When the devil had vanished, the soldier pulled off his left boot and said, “we will play the charcoal-burner a trick; just give me your knife, friend.”
sentences.n: “Kohlenbrenner”, charcoal-burner, is another sooty nickname for the devil. “einem eine Nase drehen” is to twist someone a nose — to make a fool of him; and “Gevatter” is used here simply as a familiar form of address between men.

sentences.t: Er schnitt von dem Stiefel die Sohle ab und stellte ihn neben den Hügel in das hohe Gras an den Rand einer halb überwachsenen Grube.
sentences.l: He cut the sole off from the boot and set it beside the mound in the high grass at the edge of a half-overgrown pit.
sentences.i: He cut the sole off the boot and set it down beside the mound, in the tall grass at the edge of a half-overgrown pit.
sentences.n: “abschneiden” is separable: “schnitt … ab”. The pit under the grass is planted here without comment and does the tale’s work later.

sentences.t: „So ist alles gut“ sprach er, „nun kann der Schornsteinfeger kommen.“
sentences.l: “So everything is good,” said he, “now the chimney-sweep can come.”
sentences.i: “Now all is well,” he said, “now the chimney-sweep may come.”
sentences.n: Another sooty name for the devil, after the charcoal-burner — the soldier never once calls him by a serious one.

sentences.t: Beide setzten sich und warteten, es dauerte nicht lange, so kam der Teufel und hatte ein Säckchen Gold in der Hand.
sentences.l: Both sat down and waited, it did not last long, then came the devil and had a little sack of gold in his hand.
sentences.i: The two sat down and waited; it was not long before the devil came with a little sack of gold in his hand.
sentences.n: “es dauerte nicht lange, so kam …” — German joins the two clauses with “so” where English needs “before”. “Säckchen” is the diminutive of Sack.

sentences.t: „Schüttet es nur hinein,“ sprach der Soldat und hob den Stiefel ein wenig in die Höhe, „das wird aber nicht genug sein.“
sentences.l: “Just pour it in,” said the soldier and lifted the boot a little into the height, “but that will not be enough.”
sentences.i: “Just pour it in,” said the soldier, raising the boot a little, “but it will not be enough.”
sentences.n: “nur” in an order is not “only” but “just, go ahead”. “hinein” gives the direction, inward and away from the speaker.

sentences.t: Der Schwarze leerte das Säckchen, das Gold fiel durch und der Stiefel blieb leer.
sentences.l: The Black One emptied the little sack, the gold fell through and the boot stayed empty.
sentences.i: The Black One emptied the little sack, the gold fell through, and the boot stayed empty.
sentences.n: “der Schwarze”, the Black One, is the fourth name the tale gives the devil in as many pages, all of them from soot and darkness.

sentences.t: „Dummer Teufel,“ rief der Soldat, „es schickt nicht: habe ich es nicht gleich gesagt?
sentences.l: “Stupid devil,” called the soldier, “it does not do: did I not say so at once?
sentences.i: “Stupid devil,” cried the soldier, “it will not do — did I not say so straight away?
sentences.n: “es schickt nicht” — it is not fitting, it will not answer; the impersonal use of sich schicken without the reflexive pronoun is older usage.

sentences.t: kehrt nur wieder um und holt mehr.“
sentences.l: just turn round again and fetch more.”
sentences.i: just turn back and fetch more.”
sentences.n: “kehrt … um” is umkehren, to turn back, in the plural imperative; “holt” is likewise an order, from holen, to fetch.

sentences.t: Der Teufel schüttelte den Kopf, gieng und kam nach einer Stunde mit einem viel größeren Sack unter dem Arm.
sentences.l: The devil shook the head, went and came after an hour with a much bigger sack under the arm.
sentences.i: The devil shook his head, went off, and came back an hour later with a much bigger sack under his arm.
sentences.n: German says “den Kopf” and “unter dem Arm” where English insists on “his” — the possessor is understood from the subject.

sentences.t: „Nur eingefüllt,“ rief der Soldat, „aber ich zweifle, daß der Stiefel voll wird.“
sentences.l: “Just filled in,” called the soldier, “but I doubt that the boot becomes full.”
sentences.i: “Just pour it in,” cried the soldier, “but I doubt the boot will fill.”
sentences.n: A bare past participle used as a command, with no verb at all — clipped, soldierly German that has no exact English shape.

sentences.t: Das Gold klingelte als es hinab fiel, und der Stiefel blieb leer.
sentences.l: The gold jingled as it fell down, and the boot stayed empty.
sentences.i: The gold jingled as it fell, and the boot stayed empty.
sentences.n: “hinab fiel” is printed as two words where modern spelling joins them: hinabfiel.

sentences.t: Der Teufel blickte mit seinen glühenden Augen selbst hinein und überzeugte sich von der Wahrheit.
sentences.l: The devil looked in himself with his glowing eyes and convinced himself of the truth.
sentences.i: The devil looked in himself with his glowing eyes and satisfied himself that it was so.
sentences.n: “sich überzeugen von” is to convince oneself of something — German makes the seeing-for-oneself explicit and reflexive.

sentences.t: „Ihr habt unverschämt starke Waden“ rief er und verzog den Mund.
sentences.l: “You have shamelessly strong calves,” he called and twisted his mouth.
sentences.i: “Your calves are outrageously thick,” he cried, pulling a face.
sentences.n: “Waden” are the calves of the leg — the devil is complaining about the size of the boot he is filling. “den Mund verziehen” is to pull one’s mouth out of shape.

sentences.t: „Meint ihr,“ erwiederte der Soldat, „ich hätte einen Pferdefuß wie ihr? seit wann seid ihr so knauserig?
sentences.l: “Do you think,” replied the soldier, “that I had a horse’s hoof like you? since when are you so stingy?
sentences.i: “Do you suppose,” replied the soldier, “that I have a horse’s hoof like yours? Since when are you so stingy?
sentences.n: The cloven or horse’s hoof is the devil’s one feature he cannot hide, and the soldier knows exactly whom he is talking to. “hätte” is the subjunctive of reported speech, which is why the German verb is not “habe”.

sentences.t: macht daß ihr mehr Gold herbeischafft, sonst wird aus unserm Handel nichts.“
sentences.l: see that you bring more gold here, otherwise nothing will come of our bargain.”
sentences.i: see that you bring up more gold, or nothing will come of our bargain.”
sentences.n: “macht daß …” is a plain order: see to it that. “herbeischaffen” is separable, to get something brought to the spot.

sentences.t: Der Unhold trollte sich abermals fort.
sentences.l: The fiend trotted himself off once again.
sentences.i: The fiend took himself off once more.
sentences.n: “sich trollen” is contemptuous — to shuffle or trot away. “abermals” is the older “once again”.

sentences.t: Diesmal blieb er länger aus, und als er endlich erschien, keuchte er unter der Last eines Sackes, der auf seiner Schulter lag.
sentences.l: This time he stayed away longer, and when he at last appeared, he panted under the load of a sack that lay on his shoulder.
sentences.i: This time he was longer away, and when he did appear at last he was panting under the weight of a sack that lay on his shoulder.
sentences.n: “ausbleiben” is separable, to fail to appear, to stay away. “keuchen” is to gasp for breath under a weight.

sentences.t: Er schüttete ihn in den Stiefel, der sich aber so wenig füllte als vorher.
sentences.l: He poured it into the boot, which however filled itself as little as before.
sentences.i: He poured it into the boot, which filled no more than it had before.
sentences.n: “so wenig … als” — the 1857 text uses “als” in comparisons where modern German uses “wie”.

sentences.t: Er ward wüthend und wollte dem Soldat den Stiefel aus der Hand reißen,
sentences.l: He became furious and wanted to tear the boot out of the soldier’s hand,
sentences.i: He grew furious and made to tear the boot out of the soldier’s hand,
sentences.n: “wüthend” is the 1857 spelling of wütend. “dem Soldat” takes a shortened dative without the -en the noun would normally carry.

sentences.t: aber in dem Augenblick drang der erste Strahl der aufgehenden Sonne am Himmel herauf und der böse Geist entfloh mit lautem Geschrei.
sentences.l: but at that moment the first ray of the rising sun pressed up in the sky and the evil spirit fled with loud screaming.
sentences.i: but at that moment the first ray of the rising sun came up in the sky, and the evil spirit fled with a loud cry.
sentences.n: “drang … herauf” is heraufdringen, to force its way up. Sunrise ends the devil’s claim, exactly as the three nights of watching were meant to.

sentences.t: Die arme Seele war gerettet.
sentences.l: The poor soul was saved.
sentences.n: Four words carry the point of the whole tale: the watch was kept for the sake of the dead man’s soul, and the greed that made him rich did not in the end keep him.

sentences.t: Der Bauer wollte das Gold theilen, aber der Soldat sprach „gib den Armen was mir zufällt:
sentences.l: The farmer wanted to divide the gold, but the soldier said “give the poor what falls to me:
sentences.i: The farmer wanted to divide the gold, but the soldier said, “give what falls to me to the poor;
sentences.n: “zufallen” is to fall to someone as their share; it takes the dative, here “mir”. “den Armen” is the plural of the poor used as a noun.

sentences.t: ich ziehe zu dir in deine Hütte und wir wollen mit dem übrigen in Ruhe und Frieden zusammen leben, so lange es Gott gefällt“.
sentences.l: I will move in with you into your cottage and we will live together with the rest in peace and quiet, so long as it pleases God”.
sentences.i: I am moving in with you, into your cottage, and we will live on the rest together in peace and quiet, as long as it pleases God”.
sentences.n: “zu jemandem ziehen” is to move in with someone. The closing quotation mark is printed before the full stop here, which is not how the rest of the tale sets its speech.

glossary.achte: acht — eight (numeral, inflected; achte Malter: eight Malter)
glossary.annehmen: annehmen — to accept, take (infinitive; separable an-)
glossary.arm: arm — poor (adjective; der Arme: the poor man). Also der Arm — arm (unter dem Arm: under his arm)
glossary.arme: arme — poor (arm, inflected); der Arme — the poor man (arm substantivized)
glossary.armen: der Arme — the poor man; die Armen — the poor (arm ‘poor’ substantivized; dat./gen.)
glossary.begab: sich begeben — betook himself, made his way (3rd sg. past)
glossary.bekümmert: sich bekümmern um — concerned oneself with, troubled oneself about (past part.)
glossary.bösen: der Böse — the Evil One, the devil (böse ‘wicked’ substantivized; den Bösen)
glossary.deinigen: die Deinigen — your own people, your family (substantivized possessive, dat. pl.)
glossary.drehen: drehen — to turn, twist (einem eine Nase drehen: to make a fool of someone)
glossary.erwiesen: sich erweisen — shown himself (to be) (past part.; sich mildthätig erweisen: to prove charitable)
glossary.erzeigt: erzeigen — shown, done (past part.; jemandem Gutes erzeigen: to do someone a kindness)
glossary.es: es — it; also the impersonal subject where English needs “there” or a dummy “it” (es klopfte: there was a knocking)
glossary.fetten: fett — fat (adj., inflected; die fetten Kühe)
glossary.guter: gut — good (adj., masc. nom.; mein guter Freund)
glossary.hab: haben — (I) have (1st sg. present, shortened hab)
glossary.haderlumpen: der Haderlumpen — ragamuffin, tattered fellow (Hader and Lumpen both mean rag; said of a person)
glossary.hob: heben — lifted, raised (3rd sg. past; in die Höhe heben: to lift up)
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, for him; also “to it” for a masculine or neuter noun (dative of er/es)
glossary.junge: der Junge — the lad, the boy (masc. noun; the adjective jung, young, is spelled the same)
glossary.kehrt: umkehren — turn back (2nd pl. imperative; separable um-: kehrt … um)
glossary.leben: leben — to live (infinitive; zusammen leben: to live together)
glossary.milde: die Milde — mildness, mercy (noun, f., gen. sg.; from mild)
glossary.pfeifen: das Pfeifen — whistling, a whistle (the infinitive pfeifen, to whistle, used as a noun)
glossary.reich: reich — rich (adjective; das Reich, kingdom, is a different word with the same spelling)
glossary.reiche: der Reiche — the rich man (reich ‘rich’ substantivized)
glossary.reichen: der Reiche — the rich man (dat. sg.; zu dem Reichen: to the rich man)
glossary.schwarze: der Schwarze — the Black One, i.e. the devil (schwarz ‘black’ substantivized)
glossary.schüttet: schütten — pour, tip (2nd pl. imperative; hineinschütten: to pour in)
glossary.soldaten: der Soldat — soldier (gen./dat. sg., weak noun; Sache des Soldaten: a soldier’s business)
glossary.starke: stark — strong (adj., inflected; starke Waden: thick calves)
glossary.stände: bevorstehen — would be at hand, lay ahead (3rd sg. subjunctive II; separable bevor-)
glossary.sucht: suchen — (you) seek, are looking for (2nd pl. present; was sucht ihr hier?)
glossary.wagen: wagen — to venture, to risk (infinitive; es wagen: to chance it)
glossary.wann: wann — when (interrogative; seit wann: since when)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (I) know (1st sg. present; the spelling is also the adjective weiß, white)
glossary.ziehe: ziehen — (I) move, go (1st sg. present; zu jemandem ziehen: to move in with someone)
